strengths: Novel and timely problem formulation: the paper introduces 'exploratory causal inference'—discovering unknown treatment effects from high-dimensional indirect measurements in RCTs—and is, to my knowledge, the first to connect sparse autoencoders on foundation-model representations with statistical causal testing. This is a genuinely new intersection of interpretability and causal inference.

The 'Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' is a clear, well-motivated observation, formalized in simple but correct results (Theorems 3.1/3.2) showing that significance collapse is inevitable with entangled representations as n or effect size grows. This cleanly motivates the method.

The proposed Neural Effect Search (NES) is a sensible, principled recursive stratification procedure, with a nontrivial consistency result (Appendix A) that carefully separates identification (randomization/SUTVA), estimation (post-stratification), and selection (principal-max alignment) conditions. The appendix also honestly discusses when optional residualization helps or hurts.

Reasonably thorough empirical support: a semi-synthetic benchmark with ground truth across sample sizes and effect magnitudes, ablations (no-effect case, per-round gate choice, AIPW vs. associational difference), and a real-world ecological RCT (ISTAnt) where the method recovers a behavior (grooming) known to be affected by prior rationalist analysis, plus an explicable confound (background artifact).

The paper is well written, positions itself carefully against causal feature learning, causal representation learning, and SAE-based hypothesis generation (e.g., HypotheSAEs), and includes unusually honest limitations and ethics statements, plus code and implementation details supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The consistency guarantee for NES rests on strong and arguably unrealistic assumptions (A.1 full column rank of effect directions; A.2 'principal-max' dominance and a global margin condition Γ > 2ε; A.3 additive arm-wise leakage with bounded transport error). These assumptions largely build the conclusion in—each round selects exactly one 'principal' neuron—so the theory provides limited insight beyond the toy regime where effects are nearly disjoint and one coordinate per factor strictly dominates.

The empirical validation is narrow: the semi-synthetic setting uses only r=2 binary effects on CelebA attributes with a single FM (SigLIP) and one SAE configuration. Scalability to many correlated effects, continuous outcomes, higher leakage, and multiple FMs is untested. The real-world showcase is a single experiment with n=44 videos and no quantitative comparison against alternative discovery baselines.

Baselines are weak and generic (Bonferroni, FDR, plain t-test, top-k). No comparison to other interpretable/hypothesis-generation methods (e.g., HypotheSAEs-style correlation-based discovery, clustering-based causal feature learning, or CATE-based subgroup discovery adapted to the outcome-discovery setting), making it hard to judge NES's practical advantage beyond the specific entanglement-paradox regime.

Ground-truth evaluation in the semi-synthetic experiments is defined via the best-F1 SAE neuron per attribute; this circularity (evaluating discovered codes against codes selected for their predictive alignment) could inflate apparent precision/IoU. Sensitivity of conclusions to this evaluation choice is not analyzed.

Statistical validity of the recursive procedure in finite samples is underexplored: Bonferroni control is applied per round but there is no explicit family-wise-error control across the full recursive path, and stratifying on post-treatment SAE codes raises potential collider/'bad control' concerns that are handled only at the level of assumptions rather than diagnostics. The no-effect ablation partially reassures, but a formal finite-sample FWER analysis or empirical calibration study would strengthen the claims.

The framework is restricted to binary treatments and binary outcomes, and relies on strong untestable premises (FM sufficiency for the unknown outcome, approximate SAE identifiability), which the authors acknowledge; this limits the demonstrated scope to a fairly specific class of trials.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting and underexplored problem: unsupervised discovery of unknown treatment effects in randomized trials using foundation model representations, rather than testing a pre-specified hypothesis. The framing of 'exploratory causal inference' and the rationalist/empiricist distinction is thought-provoking.

The identified problem of 'significance collapse' (multiple-testing flagging all entangled neurons as power grows) is clearly articulated and motivating, and the Neural Effect Search (NES) procedure is a simple, sensible remedy (recursive stratification with residualization on discovered effects).

The theoretical analysis is transparent: the consistency result (Theorem 4.1 / Appendix A.3) makes its assumptions explicit, discusses them, and includes an honest treatment of when residualization helps or hurts (finite-sample vs. asymptotic behavior).

Evaluation covers complementary settings: a semi-synthetic benchmark with known ground truth, a zero-effect ablation, ablations on the per-round test gate, and an AIPW vs. associational-difference comparison. The real-world ISTAnt case demonstrates the pipeline end-to-end, and the paper is commendably honest that the second discovered neuron is a background artifact and that F1 against expert labels is imperfect.
Reproducibility is reasonable: algorithm pseudocode, a minimal Python implementation, hyperparameter tables, and a code submission are provided, with public datasets.
weaknesses: The headline 'paradox' (Theorems 3.1/3.2) is essentially a restatement of the fact that statistical power tends to 1 as n or the effect size grows, so every neuron with nonzero effect is eventually rejected. This is a well-known and nearly trivial property of hypothesis testing; formalizing it as a 'paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' overstates the theoretical contribution.

The consistency guarantee for NES rests on strong and practically unverifiable assumptions: full column rank of effect directions, a 'Principal-Max alignment' condition with a strict margin Γ > 2ε, an arm-wise ε-leakage decomposition with vanishing transport discrepancy, and FM sufficiency plus the linear representation hypothesis. In real high-dimensional data, nothing guarantees that SAE codes align one-per-outcome with a dominant coordinate, so the theorem provides limited practical assurance.

The semi-synthetic evaluation is a toy setup: only r = 2 binary effects tied one-to-one to CelebA attributes (eyeglasses, wearing_hat), a single synthetic covariate, and ground-truth 'affected neurons' defined by the best-F1 SAE code against those same labels, which is somewhat circular. There is no evidence the method scales to many effects, continuous outcomes, correlated or overlapping effects, or realistic effect-hierarchy structures.

The real-world validation is thin: a single trial with n = 44, where NES returns only two neurons, one of which recovers a previously known effect (F1 = 0.398) and the other is a background/batch artifact. This does not convincingly support the claim of 'the first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial'; the artifact finding is presented as a strength but mainly shows the method detects confounds, not causal biological effects.

NES is a greedy peeling procedure with no finite-sample error control: after the first Bonferroni-gated selection, there is no guarantee on false discovery across the recursive rounds under departures from the idealized assumptions, and no comparison against alternative disentanglement or latent-variable baselines (e.g., causal representation learning or clustering approaches the paper itself cites), only against vanilla Bonferroni/FDR/t-test/top-k.

Significance of the contribution is moderate: the method is a fairly direct combination of existing components (frozen FM, SAE, post-stratified difference-in-means, Bonferroni) and the paper itself concedes it can currently only serve 'as a rescue system for hypotheses they may have missed', which limits immediate impact for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: identifying causal effects from high-dimensional, unlabeled outcomes in randomized trials, framed through the lens of SAEs as interpretable measurement channels; to my knowledge this is indeed the first serious attempt to combine SAEs with causal inference, distinct from HypotheseSAes-style correlation-based hypothesis generation.

Clear formalization of an important failure mode: the 'Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' (Theorems 3.1/3.2 showing that Bonferroni-corrected testing collapses as power grows when representations are entangled) is a simple but genuinely insightful characterization, with a clean numerical illustration in Figure 3.

The proposed Neural Effect Search (NES) is technically grounded: recursive stratification with Bonferroni control, with a consistency theorem proved under explicit assumptions (A.1-A.3), a detailed appendix proof, and an honest discussion of the margin/rank conditions, plus careful treatment of optional residualization (estimation noise, signal leakage, cross-fitting recommendation).

Reasonably thorough evaluation: semi-synthetic CelebA experiments with known ground truth across grids of sample size and effect size, comparisons against Bonferroni, FDR, vanilla t-test, and top-k, plus three ablations (no-effect, testing gate choice, AIPW vs. associational difference) and qualitative interpretability checks of the SAE codes.

Real-world demonstration on the ISTAnt ant-immunity trial recovering the known grooming effect plus a plausible background confound, with honest caveats that findings require expert interpretation; good reproducibility posture (code, minimal implementation snippet, public datasets).
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is limited: the semi-synthetic benchmark is essentially a toy (r=2 binary effects, one exogenous covariate, perfectly matched images), and the single real-world case study has n=44 videos with only two returned neurons; the practical utility of NES on realistic trials with many weak/continuous effects remains untested.

Strong and partly untestable assumptions: FM sufficiency, approximately linear concept encoding, full-rank effect directions, principal-neuron alignment, and bounded epsilon-leakage after stratification; the authors acknowledge SAE identifiability theory is immature, so the gap between the consistency theorem and practice is not fully bridged empirically.

Interpretability of the claimed empirical contribution is thin in places: in the ISTAnt experiment, NES without Bonferroni correction returns only two codes, and validation of the second (background) finding rests on a small-sample correlation with treatment; there is no systematic sensitivity analysis of the SAE training setup (m, top-k, layers) on the discovered effect set.

The contrast with related work (causal feature learning, causal representation learning with interventions) is argued mostly at the conceptual level; there is no empirical baseline comparison to the closest competing approaches (e.g., CFL-style clustering), only to generic multiple-testing corrections.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial' rests on agreement with a previously known result rather than a new scientific discovery; statistical validity of the iterative procedure (adaptive selection across rounds) is addressed asymptotically but finite-sample error control of the overall loop is not empirically characterized.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: 'exploratory causal inference' — discovering unknown treatment effects in high-dimensional, indirect measurements of RCTs — is clearly differentiated from prediction-powered causal inference and causal representation learning, and the rationalist/empiricist framing is engaging and precise.

The 'Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' (significance collapse with sample size / effect magnitude) is a genuinely interesting and correct observation, formalized in Theorems 3.1-3.2 with clean proofs, and empirically illustrated (Figure 3).

Neural Effect Search is a sensible and principled algorithmic response: recursive stratification on already-discovered effect directions to peel off entangled effects one at a time, with a consistency guarantee (Theorem 4.1) whose assumptions (rank, alignment, principal margin, bounded leakage) are explicitly stated and discussed.

Unusually thorough empirical validation for this type of paper: extensive ablations over foundation model (SigLIP/DINOv2), SAE dimension, sparsity nonlinearity (including an honest failure case with JumpReLU where assumptions break), seeds, propensity scores, opposite-effect magnitudes, zero-effect null calibration, residualization, AIPW estimator, and additional CFL-inspired LASSO/stability-selection baselines.

A real-world randomized trial (ISTAnt, ant social immunity) is analyzed end-to-end without supervision; the retrieved neurons are validated against biologist judgments (grooming F1=0.398; background marking F1=0.568), including recovering a known experimental design artifact, which is a convincing demonstration of practical utility.
Strong reproducibility practices: public datasets, detailed hyperparameters, minimal Python implementation, and an explicit ethics/limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The consistency guarantee rests on strong, practically unverifiable assumptions: full-rank effect directions, a distinct 'principal neuron' per effect with a strict population margin (Γ > 2ε), additive mean structure, and vanishing pooled-strata transport error (Assumption A.3). The authors themselves validate these only with ground-truth labels in the semi-synthetic setting and admit no unsupervised test exists; in the real trial, validity is unassessable.

The semi-synthetic benchmark is somewhat artificial: latent outcomes are defined as binary CelebA attributes mapped one-to-one onto images, with only r=2 effects and a single binary modifier W. This makes the 'perfect alignment' regime achievable by construction, so the empirical results may overstate how often the assumptions hold on genuinely complex scientific data.

The real-world demonstration has limited scope: n=44 videos, two discovered neurons, and quantitative validation reduced to F1 scores against a handful of expert annotations. The second discovery (background palette marking) is a design artifact, so the scientific yield is essentially one behavior — encouraging but thin evidence that the pipeline yields novel scientific findings at scale.

Baselines are mostly naive (t-test, Bonferroni, FDR, top-k, LASSO variants). No comparison to stronger representation-space discovery methods (e.g., HypotheSAEs with a follow-up testing step, or other residualization-based multi-testing schemes), making it harder to gauge how much of the gain comes specifically from recursive stratification versus any greedy residual approach.

The recursive procedure is greedy and sequential: a missed or mis-selected leading effect in early rounds (low-power regimes) can propagate errors; the paper discusses this but the theory offers no finite-sample guarantees, and the practical behavior under assumption violations is only partially explored.

Scope is narrow in one respect: only binary treatments, binary latent outcomes, and mean-level contrasts are considered; continuous concepts, which the authors admit SAE identifiability cannot yet handle, limit general applicability.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated problem framing: exploratory causal inference where the outcome itself is latent and must be discovered from high-dimensional measurements, formalized as a distinct setting from prediction-powered causal inference.

The proposed Neural Effect Search (NES) is a sensible and implementable procedure (recursive stratification with Bonferroni control), and a consistency result (Theorem 4.1) is provided under explicit assumptions.
The semi-synthetic CelebA benchmark has known ground truth for the affected codes, enabling quantitative Precision/Recall/IoU evaluation against multiple baselines.

Extensive supplementary experiments: encoder ablations (SigLIP, DINOv2), SAE dimension and nonlinearity sweeps, seed replicas, alternative testing gates, residualization, AIPW estimator, unbalanced propensity, and zero-effect controls.

The real-world ISTAnt trial analysis honestly reports a design artifact (background marking) alongside a biologically meaningful effect, and the authors are candid about limitations (identifiability, SAE assumptions).
weaknesses: Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 ('paradox of exploratory causal inference') are largely trivial restatements of a well-known fact: any nonzero alternative is rejected with probability tending to one as power grows, even with Bonferroni correction. Framing this as a novel paradox overstates the contribution.

The consistency guarantee for NES rests on very strong and largely unverifiable assumptions (full column rank effect directions, strict 'principal neuron' alignment with a margin Γ > 2ε, additive mean structure with bounded ε-leakage). The authors themselves demonstrate in Appendix E that a JumpReLU SAE violates the principal alignment assumption and 'NES has no guarantees' — meaning validity hinges on properties of the learned representation that cannot be checked without ground truth in the very settings where the method is intended to be used.

Conditioning/stratifying on post-treatment SAE codes Z_S is statistically delicate (collider/bad-control territory). The proof handles this via an assumed bounded 'transport error' (Assumption A.3, Eq. 30) whose magnitude is not estimable in practice; the claimed FWER/FDR control of the full recursive procedure is only asymptotic and conditional on these assumptions.

Real-world evidence is thin: a single trial with n = 44 videos, only two neurons returned, one of which is a confounded design artifact (F1 = 0.568 for a dish-position marking). The claim of 'the first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial' is supported by essentially one interpretable finding that was already known from prior work on the same dataset.

Evaluation ground truth in the semi-synthetic experiments is partly circular: 'true' affected codes are defined via the best-predicting SAE neuron for each CelebA attribute (argmax F1), so evaluation inherits the same representational assumptions the theory requires rather than independently validating them.

Baselines are comparatively weak (t-test, Bonferroni, FDR, top-k; LASSO variants added only in the appendix); no comparison against stronger representation-based discovery or selective-inference methods, and no demonstration that NES outperforms a simple stepwise regression of T on Z.

The method adds one effect per round with Bonferroni α/m gates, raising power concerns for weak secondary effects in realistic sample sizes; the paper acknowledges weaker effects can be missed but does not quantify this trade-off theoretically.

Writing/positioning issues: heavy branding (title pun, 'Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' named after the paper's framing), several typos ('a exploratory', 'loosing', 'scientists are based by'), and significant experimental content relegated to the appendix that is needed to assess the claims.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper formalizes 'exploratory causal inference' (discovering which latent outcomes are affected when the outcome is only measured indirectly through high-dimensional data), clearly distinguishing it from classical and prediction-powered causal inference. This is a genuinely new and relevant problem at the intersection of causal inference, foundation models, and interpretability.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper identifies and formalizes a real statistical phenomenon (the 'Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' — significance collapse as power grows with entangled representations) via Theorems 3.1 and 3.2, and provides a consistency guarantee for Neural Effect Search (Theorem 4.1) with a careful, structured proof in the appendix including explicit assumptions (A.1-A.3), a convergence-rate statement, and discussion of optional residualization and its finite-sample caveats.

Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: the semi-synthetic CelebA benchmark has known ground truth and includes appropriate baselines (Bonferroni, FDR, t-test, top-k, plus LASSO/stability-selection baselines inspired by causal feature learning). The ablation coverage is unusually thorough: varying foundation model (SigLIP vs DINOv2), SAE dimension (4x-16x), SAE nonlinearity (top-k and JumpReLU), random seeds, sample size, effect size, propensity imbalance, opposite-effect DGPs, a zero-effect null ablation, and explicit validation of the required representation assumptions.

Strong real-world demonstration: the ISTAnt trial application shows the pipeline end-to-end, recovering a biologically meaningful effect (grooming, in agreement with prior analyses) and a finite-sample design artifact (background marking), with domain-expert interpretation. To the authors' knowledge this is the first successful use of SAEs for causal inference on a real scientific trial, which is a notable contribution.

Honest and mature handling of limitations: the paper clearly acknowledges strong assumptions (data sufficiency, linear representation, approximate identifiability of SAEs), positions the method as a 'rescue system' complementing rather than replacing the rationalist approach, and includes a proper ethics statement.
Good reproducibility: public datasets, detailed training configurations, algorithm pseudocode (Algorithm 2), and a minimal Python implementation in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation ground truth has a potential circularity concern: in the semi-synthetic experiments, the 'ground truth neurons' are defined as the codes most predictive of CelebA attributes, which is essentially the same criterion underlying Assumption A.2 (principal alignment). This makes the benchmark somewhat favorable by construction to methods relying on principal alignment, and NES's advantage may be partly baked into the evaluation protocol.

The real-world validation (n = 44 videos) is small and largely qualitative; the quantitative evidence (F1-score = 0.398 for the grooming neuron) is modest, and the second discovered 'effect' (background marking) is a nuisance artifact rather than a scientific finding, so the practical impact of the method on real science remains to be demonstrated at scale.

The theoretical guarantees rest on strong and hard-to-verify assumptions (full column rank of effect directions, distinct principal neurons with a margin condition, bounded transport error for pooled stratification). The assumptions are validated only in the supervised semi-synthetic setting using labels, and the authors themselves note that unsupervised a-priori validation of the assumptions is an open problem; thus practical applicability to genuinely unknown settings is uncertain.

NES recovers one effect direction at a time and its consistency requires the true number of effects to be finite and the margin condition to hold per round; behavior under near-degenerate or continuously distributed effects (acknowledged as not understood for SAEs) is outside the scope, limiting generality.

Baselines are relatively simple statistical procedures or heuristics; there is no comparison with more sophisticated high-dimensional multivariate testing or knockoff-style procedures that might also handle correlated/entangled features, which would strengthen the claim that NES is the principled solution.
Scope is limited to binary outcomes and discrete treatments with two arms; extensions to continuous outcomes/concepts and multi-arm or observational settings are deferred to future work.
